title: Hasan's peace
hook: Hasan makes a treaty with Mu'awiyah to stop the bloodshed, as the Prophet ﷺ foretold (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ali's death: struck in the mosque at Kufa, and asking, the reports say, that his attacker be dealt with fairly. Your line was: fair to his killer. Who did you treat fairly when you didn't have to? Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

A boy sits beside his grandfather on the pulpit in Medina. The grandfather is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He looks out at the people, then at the boy, then out at the people again, and says something about the boy's future. This son of mine is a sayyid, a leader, and perhaps through him God will make peace between two great groups of Muslims. Bukhari keeps the scene. The boy is Hasan, Ali's elder son. And years later, after his father's death, Hasan stands at the head of an army facing another army. Today: Hasan's peace.
screen: `A BOY ON THE PULPIT.` → `THIS SON OF MINE IS A LEADER.` → `TWO GREAT GROUPS.`

segments.voice: Bukhari keeps the second scene too, in the words of a later narrator, al-Hasan al-Basri. Hasan leads armies he describes as like mountains. Facing him are the forces of Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria. One of Mu'awiyah's advisers says these armies will not turn back until each has destroyed the other. And Mu'awiyah asks a question worth hearing: if these kill those and those kill these, who will be left to look after the people, their families, their affairs? So he sends two men to Hasan, to talk. Hasan listens. And Hasan agrees to step aside and make peace. The histories report conditions in the treaty, and they differ about the details, so the details are best left to them. What Bukhari records is the outcome, and the narrator ties it straight back to the pulpit: the Prophet had said that through this son, God might make peace between two great groups. The two groups are not believers and enemies. Both are Muslims. That is what makes the moment heavy. After the Camel and Siffin, believers against believers, a grandson of the Prophet chooses to give up a claim rather than add to the graves. Muslims remember this differently, and fairly. Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam, and read the treaty as a wise and costly choice made to protect the believers when war would only have destroyed them. Sunni Muslims honor Hasan as a member of the Prophet's household and a companion, and point to this hadith as the Prophet's own praise of what he did. Tradition calls that year the year of unity. And so the part of the story that began with Ali as caliph ends here, not on a battlefield, but with a treaty.
screen: `ARMIES LIKE MOUNTAINS.` · `WHO WILL BE LEFT TO CARE FOR THE PEOPLE?` · `HASAN STEPS ASIDE.` · `BOTH GROUPS ARE MUSLIMS.` · then, large: `PEACE BETWEEN TWO GROUPS.`

segments.voice: The practice: give up a claim for peace. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one standing argument in your life. A sibling, a coworker, a neighbor, a group chat. Something where you are, quite possibly, right. Breathe in, and ask Mu'awiyah's question: if this goes on, who is left to look after the people in between? The kids, the team, the friends caught in the middle. Breathe out. You don't have to surrender anything yet. Just hold the claim in an open hand, and see what it would cost to set it down. The bell holds the time.
Hasan's peace. A grandson of the Prophet who could have fought, and instead stepped aside so two groups of Muslims would stop killing each other. Today's word.
Your line: peace between two groups. Today, in one disagreement, let go of being proven right, and notice what the other person does next. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims recall Hasan's treaty with Mu'awiyah through the hadith in Bukhari in which the Prophet calls Hasan a leader through whom God may make peace between two groups of Muslims; Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam.

myth: the two groups in the hadith were Muslims and their enemies
both were groups of Muslims. that is what made the peace so heavy.
the Prophet said this from the pulpit, with Hasan beside him
Bukhari records him looking at the people, then at the boy.
Hasan's peace was won by defeating Mu'awiyah in battle
Hasan stepped aside and made a treaty instead of fighting.

fork.setup: you're Hasan. your armies are like mountains, and so are the ones facing you. two men arrive to talk. what do you do?
options: listen, and agree to step aside for peace.
leave the army and go home alone.
fork.reveal: Hasan made peace. the narrator in Bukhari ties it to the Prophet's words: through him God would make peace between two great groups of Muslims.

original.note: Arabic: a settlement or peace treaty, the word the sources use for Hasan's agreement.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hasan simply lost the leadership.
what it means: he chose to step aside so two groups of Muslims would stop fighting, as the Prophet had hoped.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's hadith of the pulpit and the two great groups, honored by Sunni Muslims as praise of Hasan and by Shia Muslims as the second Imam's costly wisdom.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2704 (al-Hasan al-Basri's account; the Prophet on the pulpit: 'this son of mine is a sayyid… two great groups of Muslims')
al-Tabari, Tarikh (the treaty and its reported conditions; the year of unity)

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): read in full against days 877–886; facts, attributions and framing checked; no change needed.

Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm Bukhari 2704 contains the armies 'like mountains', the adviser's warning (Amr ibn al-As in the report, unnamed here), Mu'awiyah's question about who would look after the people, and the two envoys.
'Tradition calls the year that followed the year of unity' ('am al-jama'a): confirm wording and framing.

Index hook phrasing 'as the Prophet foretold' is kept as Bukhari's framing; the script says 'perhaps' as the hadith does. A Keeper may prefer different wording for Hasan's status in Sunni teaching (some Sunni scholars count his months as part of the rightly guided caliphate).
Index word is the title head 'Hasan's peace'; kept exactly.

Editor: cut 'small' (age) and the invented 'sounds like a riddle' from the hook; 'the year that followed' corrected to 'that year' for the year of unity; 'handshake' (not in the sources) changed to 'treaty'; stock carry ending ('see what grows in the space') made concrete.
